podcast.title: Sex Pistols Audition (1975)
podcast.body: In 1975, Johnny Rotten was considered for the lead singer position of the Sex Pistols after walking into Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop. His distinctive appearance, specifically wearing an "I Hate Pink Floyd" t-shirt, immediately caught attention and played a role in his consideration for the band. "Johnny Rotten walked into Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop in 1975. He was immediately considered for the job of lead singer of the sex pistols, based on the fact that he was wearing an eye-hate pink Floyd t-shirt."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fan of Trout Mask Replica
podcast.body: The future Johnny Rotten of the Sex Pistols was among the many individuals who bought and listened to Captain Beefheart's "Trout Mask Replica," specifically because of its "un-listenable" and challenging nature. "But many people, like the future Johnny Rotten of the Sex Bistels, bought it and played it because it was un-listenable."

podcast.body: Johnny Rotten, formerly of the Sex Pistols, was one of the "forefathers of punk, art rock, and new wave" who secured his first major hit song ever on a Billboard chart via the Modern Rock Chart in the late 1980s. "former sex pistol Johnny Rotten."

xref.title: Cultural Antagonism (1975)
xref.body: In 1975, a t-shirt emblazoned with "I Hate Pink Floyd" worn by Johnny Rotten played a symbolic role in his recruitment for the Sex Pistols. This demonstrated a clear generational and stylistic antagonism, with punk rock emerging in stark opposition to the established progressive rock acts like Pink Floyd. "He was immediately considered for the job of lead singer of the sex pistols, based on the fact that he was wearing an eye-hate pink Floyd t-shirt."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

It was here that he encountered Johnny Rotten, who was wearing an "I Hate Pink Floyd" t-shirt, leading to Rotten's consideration for the lead singer role in the Sex Pistols. "Johnny Rotten walked into Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop in 1975. xref.title: Formation Anecdote (1975)
xref.body: The formation of the Sex Pistols and Johnny Rotten's recruitment in 1975 is marked by a notable anecdote involving Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop. Rotten's "I Hate Pink Floyd" t-shirt served as an instant identifier of his anti-establishment attitude, leading to his consideration as the band's frontman. "He was immediately considered for the job of lead singer of the sex pistols, based on the fact that he was wearing an eye-hate pink Floyd t-shirt."

xref.title: Formation and Johnny Rotten's Audition (1975)
xref.body: In 1975, Malcolm McLaren, the former manager of The New York Dolls and co-proprietor of the "Sex" clothing shop at 430 King's Road in London's Chelsea area, sought to form a band as a living advertisement for his store. He liked the name "Pistols" for its dangerous connotation, thus "Sex Pistols." Malcolm was looking for a singer and was introduced to 19-year-old Johnny Lydon (later Johnny Rotten), who had green teeth and was spotted by Bernie Rhodes wearing a homemade "I hate Pink Floyd" t-shirt held together with safety pins. Despite Lydon's inability to sing, Malcolm had him audition by miming and "singing" Alice Cooper's "I'm 18" to a jukebox in the shop, which landed him the role. "So Malcolm got young John to audition, not caring if Johnny could actually sing a note, which he couldn't."

xref.title: Backstage Window Encounter (July 4, 1976)
xref.body: Joe Strummer of The Clash recounted how he, Johnny Rotten, and members of the Sex Pistols met The Ramones backstage at the Roundhouse by throwing a rock at a window. Johnny Ramone stuck his head out, and the British punks introduced themselves, being subsequently pulled up through the window in a "human chain" to get in. "And so they kind of formed a sort of human chain and pulled us up through this window. And that was the first time we met him and that was just a really great punk rock moment."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for British Punk (1976)
xref.body: The Ramones played a pivotal gig at the Roundhouse in London on Sunday, July 4th, 1976, as part of America's Bicentennial. Around 2,000 members of the "infant UK punk community" packed the venue, eager to hear the New York sound. This performance, along with another at Dingwalls, was immensely influential; key figures like Johnny Rotten and Joe Strummer attended soundchecks and shows, stating that the Ramones "turned them on" and "inspired them to form their own bands." The band felt like "royalty" upon arrival, noting the shift from selling out CBGB's to playing for 3,000 kids already "tuned in." "No one could have known it at the time, but this was one of the most influential gigs in the history of rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 10

xref.title: Witnessing The Ramones (July 4, 1976)
xref.body: Johnny Rotten and Sid Vicious were among the British punk figures who attended The Ramones' influential gig at the Roundhouse in London. They were "transformed by what they saw and heard," learning a lesson that contributed to the British punk rock explosion. "Johnny Rotten and Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols were there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Attacks by Monarchist Supporters (June 1977)
xref.body: On the evening of June 18, 1977, singer Johnny Rotten, along with producer Chris Thomas and engineer Bill Price, was brutally attacked by a gang armed with razors in the parking lot of London's Pegasus Hotel. Johnny Rotten claimed his thick leather pants prevented him from bleeding to death, though he sustained cuts to arm tendons that permanently hindered his ability to play guitar. The following night, drummer Paul Cook was assaulted outside a pub by six individuals wielding pipes, resulting in him needing 15 stitches to his head. "Two pistols nearly killed by monarchists."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 7

xref.title: External Pressures on the Band (Pre-1977)
xref.body: Before Matlock's departure, the Sex Pistols faced severe external pressures, including constant negative press, numerous canceled gigs, bans from most venues across the UK, and financial instability where no one was getting paid. Johnny Rotten and drummer Paul Cook had already been physically assaulted, contributing to Matlock's decision to leave. "The pistols were under constant attack by the press. Giggs were getting canceled. The group was banned for most venues across the UK. Nobody was getting paid."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Glenn Matlock's Departure (February 1977)
xref.body: Matlock's departure was officially reported as a firing in February 1977 because he "liked The Beatles too much," specifically Paul McCartney, and allegedly washed his feet too often. This narrative was fabricated and fed to the press by manager Malcolm McLaren. In truth, Matlock quit due to intense friction with Johnny Rotten, McLaren's manipulative "head games," constant media attacks, canceled gigs, venue bans, lack of pay, and the physical assaults suffered by Johnny and Paul. "Glenn Matlock was fired in February 1977... Matlock wasn't fired. He quit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Rotten's Attacks – June 1977
xref.body: Around the time "Pretty Vacant" was released, Johnny Rotten was attacked by monarchist hooligans armed with knives outside a pub called The Pegasus. His left arm was severely cut, damaging tendons to the extent that he was permanently unable to play the guitar properly. He was fortunate that his heavy leather pants deflected a blade from penetrating his thigh. Three days later, he was attacked again. "They cut up his left arm so badly that some tendons were ruined. He's never been able to play the guitar properly as a result."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joining Sex Pistols as Bassist – February 1977
xref.body: After Glenn Matlock was fired from the Sex Pistols in February 1977, manager Malcolm McLaren decided to replace him with a fan. Sid was chosen because he was always around and was Johnny Rotten's friend, embodying the punk ethos of the ultimate fan joining the ultimate band. "Malcolm McLaren came up with the idea of hiring one of the group's fans as his replacement."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Disputes with Manager Malcolm McLaren (1978)
xref.body: As the Sex Pistols gained fame, members, particularly singer Johnny Rotten, grew suspicious of Malcolm McLaren, accusing him of mismanagement of "everything, really." The band frequently found that there was no money available when they wanted to get paid. This deteriorating relationship culminated in the band's implosion at the end of a disastrous American tour in 1978.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Final Concert – January 14, 1978
xref.body: The band's last show took place at the Winterland Ballroom on January 14, 1978. A recording from that night's last song captured "the sound of a band dying violently on stage." Johnny Rotten concluded the performance with the memorable line, "Ah ha ha, have I get the feeling you've been cheated? Good night." "The last show was at the Winterland Ballroom on January 14, 1978."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Chaotic New York Concert (May 15, 1980)
xref.body: Public Image Limited (P.I.L.), led by Johnny Lydon (formerly Johnny Rotten), agreed to play two nights at the Ritz in New York for a $12,000 fee, despite internal squabbles, drug abuse, and money problems. The band was in no shape to play, lacking a drummer (the sixth one quit) and a bass player (who had just walked out). They quickly hired a 65-year-old jazz drummer from a Broadway music shop. Instead of performing live, P.I.L. pantomimed along to their records, hidden from the audience by a large screen with their silhouettes projected by bright white lights. The 1,500 people in the audience were kept waiting in the pouring rain for over an hour, then discovered the band wasn't playing, and Johnny Lydon began taunting and insulting the crowd. This led to a rain of garbage, a storming of the stage, and the destruction of all equipment, with the gig ending after just 25 minutes. "The gig was killed after just 25 minutes."

xref.title: Art School and Meeting Future Punks – Before Dropping Out
xref.body: Before dropping out of art school, Sid met John Liden (later Johnny Rotten) and John Wardle (later Jah Wobble) in his classes. He also hung out with a fourth John, John Gray, who later lived a more traditional life. "Before he dropped out of art school, John met another couple of John's in some of his classes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Catalyst for British Punk Explosion
xref.body: The Ramones' two London gigs in July 1976 are considered foundational for the British punk rock explosion. Major figures like Johnny Rotten, Sid Vicious, Joe Strummer, Chrissy Hynde, The Damned, and Billy Idol were in attendance and were profoundly "transformed by what they saw and heard," inspiring them to form their own bands. "Over the course of those two nights, July 4th and July 6th 1976, just about every single person who would become a major player in the British punk rock explosion were taught a lesson by the Ramones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Concert Ban Difficulties
xref.body: The band frequently encountered difficulties finding places to perform due to local councils banning their gigs. Johnny Rotten expressed frustration, stating that he was being denied his job while simultaneously being taxed 80% of his earnings by the very authorities that were preventing him from working. "Every time we get a gig, you get your local councils banning it and you get no complaints."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Consideration for Sex Pistols
xref.body: Following the band's exposure through "The Great Rock and Roll Swindle" soundtrack, Edward Tudor Pole was suggested as a potential replacement for Johnny Rotten in the Sex Pistols, though this never came to fruition. "And from there Edward was touted as a possible replacement for Johnny Rotten in the pistols. But that of course never happened."

xref.title: Country Life Butter Commercial
xref.body: Johnny Rotten, also known as John Lydon, from The Sex Pistols, appeared in a commercial for Country Life butter. In the ad, he humorously justified his choice not based on British heritage or rural yearning, but simply because he believed it "tastes the best." "Johnny Leiden, Mr. Ratten from The Sex Pistols, for a brand of butter."

xref.title: Early Musical Ventures
xref.body: Before joining the Sex Pistols, Sid and John Lighten (Johnny Rotten) busked, often playing Alice Cooper covers on acoustic guitar and tambourine. Their method was to play until they were paid to stop. "Sid and John Lighten picked up some spare change busking, usually by playing covers by Alice Cooper."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Final Performance and Disbandment
xref.body: The band's infamous US tour "limped" into the Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco on January 14, 1978. Running on fumes, the Sex Pistols played their final song, with Johnny Rotten's anger and frustration evident in his closing remarks: "Have I yet to feel that you've been cheated? Good night." With that, the band was officially done. "By the time the tour limped into the Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco in January the 14th, the Sex Pistols were running on fumes. And then, for the final song, they came to an end."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation After Sex Pistols Breakup
xref.body: After the Sex Pistols disbanded, Johnny Lydon (formerly Johnny Rotten) chose Jah Wobble to be the bass player for his new group, Public Image Limited. This was a risky choice due to Wobble's prickly personality. "When the Sex Fistals broke up, Johnny Liden turned to Jaw to be the bass player in his new group, Public Image Limited."

xref.title: Formation and Vision
xref.body: The Sex Pistols were formed when clothing shop owner Malcolm McLaren recruited John Lighten (who became Johnny Rotten) to be the singer for a group intended as a "living breathing advertisement" for his store, "Sex." "Malcolm McLaren recruited John Lighten to be the singer of a group that would be a living breathing advertisement for his store. He called them the Sex Pistols."

xref.title: Interview with Johnny Rotten – Before Final San Francisco Show
xref.body: Before the final Sex Pistols show in San Francisco, Sid was coherent enough to do an interview with Johnny Rotten at a local radio station. However, the interview became ugly and aggressive. "Sid was straight enough to do an interview with Johnny at a local radio station. But it got ugly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: John Lydon – Spinal Meningitis in Childhood Shaped His Personality and Punk Identity
xref.body: John Lydon (Johnny Rotten) contracted spinal meningitis as a child, which resulted in memory loss, spinal curvature, and the development of a markedly contrary and independent personality. These characteristics, forged by illness, were central to his becoming the iconic vocalist of the Sex Pistols. "Contracted spinal meningitis as a child, resulting in memory loss, a curvature of the spine, and a markedly contrary and independent personality."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Rotten's Distinctive Image
xref.body: Johnny Rotten, a customer of the "Sex" shop, was chosen to front the Sex Pistols and was notable for his menacing stare and green teeth, contributing to the band's shocking and rebellious image. "Being a kid with a menacing stare and green teeth that everybody called Johnny Rotten."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Rotten's Secret Wealth – Married to Publishing Heiress Worth ~£50 Million; Made Millions in UK Real Estate
xref.body: Despite assiduously maintaining his working-class punk image, John Lydon is married to Nora Forster, a German media and publishing heiress with an estimated net worth of approximately £50 million. They met during the Pistols' original run in the late 1970s when Lydon was about 22 and Forster was 36. Nora's daughter from a previous relationship was Ari Up, singer of The Slits — meaning Ari introduced her mother to Johnny. Additionally, unbeknownst to most punk fans, Lydon has made a considerable personal fortune by investing in the UK real estate market. "Johnny Rotten, punk by profession but secretly very, very comfortable."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Manager Malcolm McLaren's Manipulation
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren actively fostered animosity between Glenn Matlock and Johnny Rotten, setting them up to play "head games" with each other. He also created the false story of Matlock being fired for liking The Beatles, disseminating it to the press immediately after Matlock left. "Malcolm McLaren set it up so the two were always playing head games with each other."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Paul Cook's Attack
xref.body: Following Johnny Rotten's attacks, drummer Paul Cook was also assaulted with a pipe in a manner described as "all medieval on his ass." "And then someone took a pipe to drummer Paul Cook and went all medieval on his ass."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Breakup Activities of Members – Jones, Cook, Rotten
xref.body: After the breakup, guitarist Steve Jones and drummer Paul Cook went to South America and recorded with an exiled British criminal. Johnny Rotten (John Liden) traveled to Jamaica to relax, immerse himself in reggae music, and smoke ganja. "Guitar Steve Jones and drummer Paul Cook ended up in South America where they recorded with an exiled British criminal. Johnny Rotten eventually turned up in Jamaica to decompress, soak up some reggae and smoke some ganja."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Punk Scene Roots
xref.body: Born William Broad, Billy Idol was deeply immersed in the original punk rock scene, actively following the Sex Pistols and associating with seminal figures like Johnny Rotten and Sid Vicious before adopting his stage name and forming Generation X. "William Broad followed the pistols everywhere. He was deep into the original punk rock scene."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Real Name and Nickname Origin
xref.body: Sid Vicious's birth name was John Simon Richie. His friend Johnny Lydon (Johnny Rotten) gave him the nickname "Sid" after Lydon's pet hamster. The "Vicious" part of his name was inspired by a Lou Reed song. Despite being initially "quite a gentle guy," Richie felt compelled to live up to the "Vicious" title.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

xref.title: Sid Vicious's Background and Entry
xref.body: John Simon Richie, known as Sid Vicious, replaced Glenn Matlock as bass player. He was described as a violent, semi-literate hanger-on and had previously been a sometime drummer and saxophone player. Before joining the group, he worked as a shop assistant in a sex shop. He considered Johnny Rotten an "old enemy" from the start, but after seeing the band perform, he thought they were "really wonderful" and admired their honesty, citing the Bill Grundy incident as genuine. "His replacement was a violent semi-literate hangar on and sometime drummer and saxophone player named John Simon Richie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Three-Member Lineup for Recording
xref.body: For the recording of "Holidays in the Sun," The Sex Pistols were a three-piece band consisting of Johnny Rotten, Steve Jones, and Paul Cook, as bassist Glenn Matlock had been fired, requiring Steve Jones to perform the bass parts. "When the pistols recorded this next song, they were down to just three members. There was Johnny Rotten, guitarist Steve Jones and drummer Paul Cook. Bass player Glenn Matlock had been fired, so it was up to Steve to play the bass parts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: US Tour Visa Troubles
xref.body: The band faced significant difficulties obtaining working visas for their planned late 1977 American tour due to the criminal records of its members. Johnny Rotten had a minor drug charge, Steve Jones and Paul Cook had past theft charges, and Sid Vicious had a record including drug charges, assault on a police officer, attempted grand theft auto, criminal damage, and possession of a dangerous weapon. "Getting working visas for these yobbs proved to be very difficult."
